mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes GLS63 AMG engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rebuilt M177 V8 engine for the GLS63 costs £7,500-£13,500 supply-only; a rebuilt M157 V8 for earlier models costs £7,000-£11,000 supply-only. Fitting adds £1,500-£2,500 depending on complexity - AMG V8 work requires specialist knowledge.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of oil separator failure on a Mercedes GLS63?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common sign is a burning oil smell or oil dripping from the rear of the engine. A whistling noise or rough idle can also be early indicators. If ignored, oil separator failure leads to rear main seal leaks and potentially bottom-end damage.

mainEntity.name: Is the Mercedes GLS63 V8 engine (M177) reliable?

acceptedAnswer.text: The M177 is a fundamentally strong hand-built AMG V8 - one of Mercedes' most impressive modern engines. It has a small number of well-documented weak points (oil separator, rear main seal, turbocharger bearings) that are well understood by specialists. With proper maintenance, the M177 routinely exceeds 100,000 miles.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Mercedes GLS63 engine last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Properly maintained M177 V8 engines routinely reach 100,000-150,000 miles before major work, though oil separator and rear main seal issues can occur from 40,000 miles.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in my Mercedes GLS63?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the GLS63 is otherwise in good condition with no rust or major electrical faults. A rebuilt M177 costs £7,500-£13,500 - far less than replacing a £45,000-£85,000 vehicle. The GLS63's strong residual values make engine replacement financially justifiable.

mainEntity.name: What oil does my Mercedes GLS63 AMG need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mercedes-Benz specifies MB 229.5 high-performance oil - typically 5W-30 or 5W-40 fully synthetic. The M177 V8 requires approximately 9.5 litres.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes Benz GLS Class GLS63 - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The GLS63 AMG launched with the X166 generation in 2012 as the GL63 AMG, powered by the M157 5.5-litre twin-turbo V8 - a thunderous 557-585hp powerhouse carried over from the ML63. In 2019, the all-new X167 GLS63 replaced it with the M177 4.0-litre twin-turbo V8 featuring hot-vee design and, from 2023, 48V EQ Boost mild-hybrid technology. In 2026, Mercedes-AMG unveiled the comprehensively revised M177 EVO with a new flat-plane crankshaft, delivering 603hp and 627lb-ft of torque.

items.commonFailure: Oil separator failure leading to rear main seal leaks - the most frequent and expensive problem on the M177 as these vehicles accumulate mileage. The oil-vapour separator (PCV valve) can become blocked, increasing crankcase pressure and forcing oil past the weakest point - the rear main crankshaft seal (RMS). This issue has been reported across multiple M177 applications, often on low-to-mid-mileage cars. Mercedes-Benz mandates that both oil separators be replaced whenever a rear main seal is found leaking. Turbocharger bearing degradation has also been reported due to the hot-vee design.

commonProblems.h2: Mercedes Benz GLS Class GLS63 Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The GLS63's M177 twin-turbo V8 is one of AMG's most impressive modern engines - a hand-built masterpiece assembled in Affalterbach according to the "One man, one engine" philosophy. However, as these vehicles accumulate mileage, several well-documented issues can drive significant repair costs. The most frequent and expensive problem is oil separator failure, which often leads to rear main seal leaks. Every rebuilt engine supplied through EnginesMarket includes upgraded components addressing the original failure point, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.group: M177 Oil Separator Failure & Rear Main Seal Leak
problems.h4: M177 Oil Separator Failure & Rear Main Seal Leak - The Most Expensive M177 Problem
problems.rootCause: The oil-vapour separator (cyclonic separator) is a known weak point on the M177 engine. When the separator becomes blocked, crankcase pressure increases significantly, and the weakest point in the crankcase seal system - the rear main crankshaft oil seal (RMS) - fails. This can start as a whistling noise or rough idle before escalating to a blown rear main seal. Mercedes-Benz mandates that both oil separators be replaced whenever a rear main seal is found leaking to prevent repeat failure.

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical 2019-present GLS63 AMG 4MATIC+ is worth approximately £45,000-£85,000 depending on mileage and condition. The GLS63 sits firmly in the £15,000+ band - replacement cost is typically small relative to vehicle value, making a full rebuilt engine a justifiable investment for owners of these high-value performance SUVs.
problems.recommendation: The oil separator is the root cause of most M177 rear main seal leaks. If you notice oil around the transmission bellhousing, a burning oil smell, or hear a whistling noise from the engine, have the crankcase pressure checked immediately. If caught early, replacing the oil separators alone (£600-£950 at a specialist) prevents the much more expensive rear main seal replacement. If the rear main seal has already failed, replacing both the seal and the oil separators together is the only sensible approach. On a GLS63 worth £45,000-£85,000, the full rebuilt engine route is justifiable if bottom-end damage has occurred.

problems.h4: M177 Turbocharger Failure - The Hot-Vee V8's Performance Weakness
problems.rootCause: The M177's twin-turbochargers are mounted in the hot-vee configuration, subjecting them to extreme heat. Sustained high-temperature operation accelerates bearing wear, leading to oil burning and potential turbo failure. Coolant lines can also fracture due to age and heat cycles, causing cooling line failure and subsequent turbocharger failure if left unaddressed. Oil starvation is another contributing factor.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Inspect turbocharger bearings, check oil supply and coolant lines
repairOptions.longevity: If turbo noise or power loss detected early

Replace both turbochargers, inspect oil supply and return lines, replace coolant lines
repairOptions.longevity: If both turbos have failed or are high-mileage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: As above - a typical GLS63 is worth £45,000-£85,000.
problems.recommendation: Preventative maintenance is the key to avoiding M177 turbocharger failure. Use only Mercedes-spec oil (MB 229.5) and change it every 10,000 miles or 12 months - never stretch the interval. If you hear a high-pitched whistle, notice a loss of power, or see blue smoke from the exhaust, have the turbochargers inspected immediately. Coolant lines should be replaced any time they are removed. If one turbo has failed, replace both - the other will typically fail within a short period due to shared oil supply and similar operating conditions.

problems.h4: M177 Excessive Oil Consumption & Rough Idle - The V8's Long-Term Challenges
problems.rootCause: The M177 engine can suffer from excessive oil consumption, particularly if maintenance intervals have been stretched. Rough idle and vibration have also been reported, with some owners experiencing shaking at idle that persisted despite standard maintenance. Carbon buildup and oil consumption can creep in, especially if the engine wasn't maintained with regular oil changes and high-quality fluids.
